doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Jazz's decline in the 1970s and the swing revival
summary: He gives his view that jazz went underground, that pop took over its communicative role, and that Scott Hamilton, Getz and Zoot Sims, and then Wynton revived accessible jazz.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: nonsense. This saxophone player whose name I’ve just blocked out, the last of the boppers — practiced on the Brooklyn Bridge.

Sonny Rollins, I don’t know why I can’t think, Sonny Rollins. He was playing all the time, but he had sort of gone underground. I mean people didn’t hear these people. Coltrane is dead I think already, and so all of a sudden people like Stan Getz and Scott Hamilton, and Zoot Sims were sort of becoming heroes again. And it was very communicative, easy to understand music. And the public said oh, all right, I can understand that. So a lot of people who didn’t know, could understand it. So they started to embrace it again. And then along comes Wynton, who’s — gee I mean on one level he’s playing his far out music, on another level he’s playing so far in New Orleans music, march music. And God bless him. And a lot of the young guys today are very much traditionalists. You know I mean they’re acoustic bass and they’re playing. I mean they have the modern touch to it, a very modern touch and very technical, and great expertise. But jazz has sort of said, people sort of said well we’ve got to communicate. If we don’t communicate, we’re going to get lost.

Because there’s a couple of people who will get away with going out in front of huge audiences and getting out. There’s always a couple of people who can get away with it. And everybody else says hey I’m going to do that, and they can’t get an audience. Because the audience says, huh, yeah, come on, you know we’re being very kind here. We don’t understand what’s going on but these are stars. So it goes like everything, it pushes the envelope and people go — they don’t understand it. So I’m just looking at it from my parents’ standpoint, and people who buy this stuff. You know they only sell three percent of the records in the country. So who’s buying what? And if you want to make a living at it, I’m not saying sell out, God knows my kids, they’re not selling out, they’re finding out what it’s about, they’re doing their own music now. My son put out two records already. And he got wonderful reviews and he sold eleven records.
